title: The vineyard tenants (Mark 12:1–12)
hookLine: the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone

lines: A VINEYARD, A HEDGE, A TOWER.
LAST OF ALL, THE BELOVED SON.
cards: Still in the temple courts, the leaders still listening, Jesus tells a story. A man plants a vineyard. He builds a hedge around it, digs a winepress, puts up a watchtower.
Scripture readers would hear Isaiah, whose song pictured Israel as God's vineyard. The owner rents it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share.
They beat him and send him off empty. Another; they hit him on the head. Another; they kill him.
Many more, beaten or killed. He has one left: his son, his beloved. Surely they'll respect my son.

teach.b: They kill him and throw him out of the vineyard. What will the owner do? He'll come, put an end to those tenants, and give the vineyard to others.
Then Jesus quotes a psalm, in the King James Bible: "The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner."

teach.h: BEN AND EVEN: SON AND STONE.
teach.b: Picture builders tossing one stone onto the rubbish heap as useless; later, that very stone holds the corners of the whole building together.

It's Psalm 118, the same psalm the crowds sang days earlier: blessed is he that cometh. Many readers point out a wordplay in Hebrew: son is ben, stone is even. The son they reject becomes the stone everything rests on.
Christians hear the whole story of Jesus in it: sent last, beloved, rejected, killed, and made the cornerstone.
Mark says the leaders understood he'd told it against them, and wanted to arrest him, but feared the crowd, so they left.

teach.h: AIMED AT A FEW, NOT A PEOPLE.
teach.b: This parable has sometimes been misused to claim God rejected the Jewish people. Mark points it at a handful of leaders, while the crowd, Jewish too, stands with Jesus.
Many churches today say plainly that the anti-Jewish reading is wrong. Now look back at the week. Ransom, and not to be served but to serve.
Bartimaeus and what do you want. A borrowed colt. A fig tree and a temple.
Faith that moves mountains, and forgive, then pray. A question answered with a question.

teach.h: THE STONE WHICH THE BUILDERS REJECTED IS BECOME THE HEAD OF THE CORNER.
teach.b: And the rejected stone. All week the road has led to one place, and the stone is part of what waits there.

how: Christians often call Jesus the cornerstone, drawing on this psalm, and many churches mark the laying of a building's cornerstone with a service; many churches today also teach explicitly against reading this parable as a rejection of the Jewish people.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the stone line comes from the psalm the crowd sang at his entry
Psalm 118: blessed is he that cometh, and the rejected stone.
Mark aims the parable at the Jewish people as a whole
Mark says the leaders knew it was told against them; the crowd stood with Jesus.
the son was the first one sent
servant after servant first. the beloved son last of all.

games.q: you're the owner of a vineyard. the tenants have beaten or killed every servant you sent. you have one beloved son left. what do you do?
o: send the son: surely they'll respect him.
games.why: he sends the son: "They will reverence my son." they kill him. and the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner.

practice: Think of someone others tend to overlook: the colleague whose ideas get talked over, the neighbor nobody visits, someone the builders tossed on the pile.
Ask what they hold up that nobody notices, and what it would look like to value them out loud. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Even, the Hebrew word for stone, echoing ben, son, in Psalm 118. The rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone.

orig.note: Hebrew: stone, in Psalm 118:22. many hear a wordplay with ben, son.

carryVoice: Your line: the rejected stone. The one tossed aside ends up holding the corners. That's the week.

sources.q: The stone which the builders rejected is become the head of the corner
